newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo economic growth hampered by lack of IMF deal.
newsitem.headline: Yugo economic growth hampered by lack of IMF deal.

text.p: Yugoslavia's readmission to International Monetary Fund (IMF) will not be settled before June 1997 and economists said on Monday the country was heading for another year without external borrowing needed for growth.

"The IMF has opted for another six-month delay to decide on Yugoslavia's membership in the Fund. This means no IMF funds until the end of 1997," Pavle Petrovic, chief economist of the CES-Mecon private economic research institute, told Reuters.
"Without the IMF deal, Yugoslavia will probably not be able to borrow from other financial institutions," he said.

Yugoslavia, now a federation of Serbia and Montenegro, had to apply for restoration of its IMF seat which was suspended under UN sanctions during the Bosnian war. But the IMF postponed a decision earlier this month, the eighth such postponment since June 14, 1993

Economic planners have forecast the 1997 GDP growth rate at 13 percent, but economists cautioned even a six percent growth would be difficult to achieve without foreign finance, sweeping privatisation and deep restructuring.
The country's economy has progressed for several years at a slower pace than the predictions by the economic planners with GDP increasing annually by an average 5-6 percent since 1994.
Economists agree double-digit growth rates could be achieved only with the inflow of foreign investment.
Without external funds, it will be difficult even to repeat the 1996 performance, an economy professor said.
"For several years, we have barely managed to survive," said Jurij Bajec, also a member of the Economics Institute.
He insisted that the mechanisms of restrictive monetary and fiscal policy were exhausted.
"Without serious privatisation and restructuring, 1997 targets will be beyond the reach."

To achieve the 1996 growth rate between 6-7 percent, Yugoslavia will have to keep heavy pressure on its balance of payments. "(The balance of payments) will have to retain big deficit," Petrovic said.
Petrovic insisted Yugoslavia could rely only on hot capital to cover its balance of payments deficit.
"But hot capital is not a reliable source. During 1996, it was attracted by high interest rates on dinar funds. Any monetary easing would scare away that capital," Petrovic said.
On the other hand, Bajec cautioned an absence of the IMF deal will make things more difficult, giving local monopolies another excuse not to reform and keep the status quo.

Economists therefore urged the government to create an effective economic environment in 1997 -- to restore economic ties with the world, raise foreign trade to $7.5 billion and undertake serious privatisation and restructuring.

"Privatisation must be fast and the government should identify those industry sectors which can push the economy forward," Bajec said, adding it was encouraging that even politicians began to talk publicly about the process.
Petrovic said the government needed to step up reforms but also maintain stability. "Only then can we attract foreign investment," Petrovic said.
However, analysts feared economic progress will be stalled without a reduction in public spending and in absence of fiscal reforms.

Yugoslavia's public spending is seen at 47.5 percent of GDP in 1997, but economists said in reality it ran as high as 52 percent of the GDP. Nebojsa Savic, vice-president of the private Braca Karic University, said public spending had to come down to between 42 and 45 percent to become tolerable.

"I have suggested a gradual reduction in public spending, with 1.5 percent sliced off the total a year. But as long as public spending remains so high, companies will not be able to reduce costs and households savings will not revive," he said.
Analysts saw no quick cure to the problem and admitted any sweeping reform of public spending would be too painful and would raise a need for a health and education reform.
"But if we wait for another year or so, the problem will only worsen," Petrovic said. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
